title: Dynamic clock governor + kernel bundling for KV-cache-aware prefill/decode
creator: Marco Li
description:
Problem: For mixed-length workloads on multi-tenant GPU nodes (H100/L40S/A10 with MIG partitions) we observe suboptimal unit-economics due to conservative static clock policies and coarse kernel selection. Long prefill steps frequently evict KV-cache locality and force decode kernels to run at suboptimal clocks, increasing p95 latency and token cost.

Goal: Implement a dynamic clock governor that coordinates with the kernel selection and prefill/decode scheduler to: (1) opportunistically raise clocks for short low-latency decodes; (2) lower clocks during batch-heavy long-prefill phases while preserving throughput; (3) bundle kernel choices by KV-cache affinity to reduce cross-partition memory thrash. Deliver measurable improvements in p95 latency and per-token cost on H100/L40S and safe regressions on A10.

Approach:
- Add a clock-governor component to the runtime control plane that subscribes to scheduling decisions and kernel fingerprints.
- Compute a per-MIG-partition power/latency policy using a small online estimator (moving window) that predicts decode vs prefill dominance.
- Extend kernel selection to emit a KV-cache-affinity tag; scheduler will attempt to pack requests with matching affinity into the same execution window.
- Implement an "elastic prefill window": allow prefill to be split into high-frequency micro-prefills for short queries (reduce tail) and consolidated prefill for long sequences (improve throughput).
- Safety: governor must respect tenant SLAs and global thermal caps; provide hard ceilings and graceful fallback to static clocks.

Success metrics (bench):
- p95 decode latency down by >=10% on H100 for mixed traffic (10-90 token mixtures).
- Throughput (tokens/s) maintained +/-5% for long sequence workloads.
- Per-token GPU energy/cost reduced >=8% on L40S under typical batch distributions.
- No SLA violations for enterprise tenants during A/B test.

Artifacts and links:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Dynamic+Clock+Governor+Design
- Profiling dashboard (internal): https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/xyz/prefill-decode-profiles
- Spike PR with kernel-affinity tags: https://github.com/redwood/inference/pull/6214

Rollout plan:
1) Lab experiments on dedicated H100 single-tenant nodes (week 1): validate estimator and kernel-affinity tagging.
2) Canary on Dedicated pool with controlled tenants (week 2): A/B against static policy; monitor thermal and token-cost metrics.
3) Gradual ramp to multi-tenant MIG clusters (week 3): restrict aggressive clocks to non-production tiers initially.
4) Full launch with runtime-1.20 if metrics and safety gates pass.

Risks and mitigation:
- Thermal oscillation: add hysteresis and minimum dwell time for clock changes.
- Interference across MIG slices: enforce per-slice power caps and prefer intra-slice bundling.
- Kernel misclassification: keep a fallback path to the previously successful kernel and log frequency to drive offline retraining of the fingerprinting heuristic.

Open questions:
- Should the estimator use sequence-length prediction from the request layer (app-level hints) or purely runtime-observed token rates? (Trade-off: prediction accuracy vs. API surface).
- What is the safe minimum dwell time for clocks on H100 to avoid performance thrash?

Bench harness reproduces p95 improvement in lab for H100 mix
Canary runs for 48h without SLA breaches
